To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
A new empirical function is presented to estimate j(NO 2) from global radiation, independent of solar elevation and cloud conditions, with a mean absolute residual of ±0.6 % (2σ)."
a polynomial function can be used to calculate the NO2 photolytic frequency j(NO2), based on the solar global radiation G, with a precision of ±6×10−4 s−1.

1) a simple second-order polynomial function can be used to accurately estimate ground-level j( NO2) from G; 2) the relationship is valid for all atmospheric conditions, and 3) it is independent of solar zenith angles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new empirical relationship between j(NO2), the photolysis frequency of nitric oxide, and global solar irradiance (G).
the development of new approaches and tools for the analysis and visualization of large amounts of environmental data, with the goal of improving the understanding of atmospheric processes.
the study of the relationship between the NO2 photo-dissociation frequency and the global irradiance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relationship between the NO2photolysis frequency and solar global irradiance is linear.
the relationship between j(NO2)(λ) and G is not linear.
the relationship between j(NO2)(NO2) and G is linear for clear skies (α=0) but non-linear for cloudy conditions (α>0).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the empirical function is valid for a wide range of environmental conditions and is applicable for the calculation of j(NO2), and thus for air chemistry studies, in all atmospheric environments.
the empirical function can be used to calculate j(NO2) from G, and thus to estimate NOx concentrations, fluxes and deposition velocities, with a precision of 5–10%.
we can use global radiation as a proxy for the NO2 photolytic frequency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the NO2 photolytic frequency can be estimated from global radiation, which is a standard parameter in many field experiments and in most meteorological observation networks.
the empirical function provides a simple and robust tool for estimating ground-level j(NO 2) from G, which is a widely available and easily measurable parameter.
the relationship between j(NO2), G and α is independent of solar zenith angles and can thus be used for any time and location.
